passages.t: Ahaz walks in the ways of Israel's kings
passages.happening:
‘Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD’ (verse 1). He makes cast images of the Baals (verse 2). ‘Moreover, Ahaz burned incense in the Valley of Hinnom and sacrificed his sons in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites’ (verse 3). He sacrifices on the high places and under every green tree (verse 4).

The LORD gives him into the hand of the king of Aram, who takes many captives to Damascus, and into the hand of Pekah of Israel, whose army kills many in Judah in one day, ‘because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers’ (verse 6). The Israelites take 200,000 captives from their own kinsmen, women, sons and daughters, and bring them to Samaria with plunder (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
After Jotham's quiet faithfulness, his son plunges Judah to its lowest point so far. Chronicles tells his reign as a run of disasters that Ahaz meets by reaching for every help but the LORD. A common reconstruction dates him about 735 to 715 BC, though this period's chronology is much debated. Second Kings 16 tells the same reign, and Isaiah 7 tells of the prophet's meeting with Ahaz in the same crisis. Around 734 BC Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel attacked Judah, probably to force it into an alliance against Assyria.

Verse 3 names the worst thing a king could do. Sacrificing children in the fire in the Valley of Hinnom, just south of Jerusalem, was a practice the law condemned as one of the abominations of the nations. It was associated with the god Molech and with rites in times of desperate crisis. The text names it, and these notes do not describe it. The valley's Hebrew name, Ge-Hinnom, later became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for the place of final judgment.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You must not give any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech, for you must not profane the name of your God’ (Leviticus 18:21). Second Kings says of Ahaz, ‘he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel’ (2 Kings 16:3).
passages.asks: Ahaz gave his own children to an idol in a time of crisis. Ask what you have been tempted to sacrifice, in your family or in yourself, to keep yourself safe. And ask who in your care needs protecting from the pressures you are under.

passages.happening:
‘But a prophet of the LORD named Oded was there, and he went out to meet the army that returned to Samaria’ (verse 9). God gave Judah into their hand, he says, but they have killed in a rage that reaches to heaven, and now they mean to enslave their kinsmen: ‘But are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?’ (verse 10). He tells them to send the captives back (verse 11).

Leaders of Ephraim stand against the returning army: ‘For our guilt is great, and fierce anger is upon Israel’ (verse 13). The soldiers leave the captives and the plunder (verse 14). ‘Then the men who were designated by name arose, took charge of the captives, and provided from the plunder clothing for the naked. They clothed them, gave them sandals and food and drink, anointed their wounds, and put all the feeble on donkeys’ (verse 15), and bring them to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their own people.
passages.hearers:
The surprise in the middle of the chapter is that the most godly people in it are northerners: a prophet and a group of leaders in Samaria who show mercy to their kinsmen from Judah. Judah's king is faithless; leaders in Samaria, which had long since broken with the temple, confess their guilt and obey a prophet. Guilt, ashmah, comes four times in Oded's speech and the leaders' answer.

In a world where war captives were routinely enslaved, their kindness was striking: they clothe, give sandals, feed, anoint wounds and carry the weak on donkeys to Jericho. Within a few years the northern kingdom itself would fall to Assyria, in 722 BC, a fact behind Oded's warning that Israel's own guilt was great. Many readers have noticed how closely the scene resembles Jesus' story of the good Samaritan, with people from Samaria tending the wounded on the road to Jericho; whether Jesus meant an echo is debated, and the Gospel does not say.
passages.later: Jesus told of a traveler on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, and of a Samaritan who ‘went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine’ (Luke 10:34). The law had said, ‘You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart’ (Leviticus 19:17).
passages.asks: The kindest people in the story came from the side Judah thought was faithless. Ask whom you have written off who might show more mercy than you. And ask what captives, of any kind, you could help bring home.

passages.t: Help from Assyria that did not help, and the doors shut
passages.happening:
‘At that time King Ahaz sent for help from the king of Assyria’ (verse 16). Edom and the Philistines raid Judah (verses 17-18). ‘For the LORD humbled Judah because Ahaz king of Israel had thrown off restraint in Judah and had been most unfaithful to the LORD’ (verse 19). ‘Then Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came to Ahaz but afflicted him rather than strengthening him’ (verse 20). Ahaz pays him from the temple, the palace and the princes, ‘it did not help him’ (verse 21).

‘In the time of his distress, King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD’ (verse 22). He sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, saying, “Because the gods of the kings of Aram have helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me” (verse 23). ‘But these gods were the downfall of Ahaz and of all Israel’ (verse 23). He cuts up the temple's vessels, ‘shut the doors of the house of the LORD’ (verse 24), and sets up altars on every street corner. He dies and is not buried in the tombs of the kings (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The word help, azar, runs through the chapter like a thread. Ahaz sends to Assyria for help, the Assyrian king does not help him, and he sacrifices to Aram's gods so that they may help him. Earlier in Chronicles God helped faithful kings. Unfaithful, ma'al, now describes Ahaz three times. The Chronicler calls him king of Israel in verse 19, because for him Israel names the whole covenant people.

Ahaz appealed to Tiglath-pileser the Third, who crushed Damascus in 732 BC and annexed much of the northern kingdom's land. Assyrian royal inscriptions from his reign list Ahaz, under his fuller name Jehoahaz, among the western kings who paid him tribute. Tribute bought protection at the price of vassal status and pressure. Ahaz's reasoning in verse 23 reflects the common belief that a nation's success proved its gods' power.

Second Kings 16:9 says the Assyrian king responded to Ahaz and took Damascus; verse 20 here says he afflicted Ahaz rather than strengthening him. Both can stand: Kings reports the immediate military result, and Chronicles the long cost, vassalage, empty treasuries and no lasting security. Some see the Chronicler reshaping Kings to make a point about misplaced trust; others see two aspects of the same events. Either way the help Ahaz bought was not help at all. The chapter ends with the temple doors shut, and the next chapter opens them.
passages.later: Isaiah had told Ahaz, ‘Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened over these two smoldering stubs of firewood’ (Isaiah 7:4). Second Kings says, ‘So the king of Assyria responded to him, marched up to Damascus, and captured it’ (2 Kings 16:9).
passages.asks: In his distress Ahaz grew more unfaithful, not less. Ask what you reach for when things get worse. And ask whether any door to God in your life has been shut, and what it would take to open it.
